analysis.one_liner: Expands and makes permanent the tax credit for building low-income rental housing, and strips tax deductions from owners of substandard units.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have expanded a tax credit that subsidizes affordable housing, never received a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the low-income housing tax credit from 4% to 9% for federally subsidized new buildings and made the credit permanent. It would have shortened the depreciation period for low-income rental property from 27.5 years to 20, exempted low-income housing investments from the 1986 rules limiting passive tax losses, and stripped federal tax deductions from owners whose rental units violate health, safety, and building codes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters would gain if more affordable units were built and existing ones kept from converting to higher rents, which the bill's findings tied to a 70% drop in federal housing spending between 1981 and 1989 and an estimated 900,000 subsidized units at risk of loss by 1995. Real estate developers and tax-credit investors would also gain directly: a larger and permanent credit, a faster 20-year depreciation write-off, and exemption from passive loss limits all raise their after-tax returns, and owners of code-compliant units would keep their deductions while owners of substandard units lost theirs.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the low-income housing credit from 4% to 9% for new buildings that are federally subsidized, making subsidy dollars go further on new construction.
Makes the low-income housing credit permanent instead of scheduled to expire, giving developers certainty for multi-year projects.

Exempts low-income housing credit activities from the passive loss limitation and exempts interest, tax, and business-expense deductions from those limits for investors who actively manage low-income housing projects, removing a tax penalty that had discouraged individual investors.
Shortens the depreciation period on low-income rental property from 27.5 years to 20 years, increasing after-tax returns for investors who build or rehabilitate affordable units.

Denies all tax deductions, including depreciation, for rental units that are not suitable for occupancy under local health, safety, and building codes, aimed at owners who collect income from substandard units while claiming federal deductions.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole, through reduced tax revenue from the larger permanent credit, faster depreciation, and the passive loss exemptions; the bill text does not estimate the cost. Investors in low-income housing who own substandard units would pay by losing their deductions.

drawbacks.text: The bill was funded entirely through the tax code: a bigger and permanent credit, faster depreciation, and passive loss relief would all reduce federal revenue, with the size of the loss not stated in the bill.

The passive loss exemption (Section 6) would primarily benefit higher-income taxpayers with rental real estate losses to shelter, since passive loss limits were enacted in 1986 precisely to restrict such deductions.

Making the low-income housing credit permanent (Section 3) locks in a subsidy channel that runs through private investors and syndicators, who take fees and returns before any housing is built; the bill offered no direct public alternative.
Denying deductions for units not 'suitable for occupancy' depends on Treasury regulations defining suitability against local codes, leaving room for inconsistent enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its own terms, the bill traded tax revenue for more affordable housing, and it paired its investor tax breaks with a rare accountability measure—stripping deductions from owners of substandard units—that made the incentives conditional on decent conditions. Its main weakness is structural: it funneled the public investment through tax-credit investors and developers, a channel widely criticized as delivering fewer homes per dollar than direct subsidy would, and the passive loss and depreciation provisions would have enriched investors regardless of how much new housing resulted. It died in committee, so none of this was ever weighed in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on November 22, 1991 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — for the remaining fourteen months of the 102nd Congress.
The bill never advanced past committee and received no vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue it would have given up, and owners of substandard rental housing kept their deductions. No new low-income housing incentives were created, so renters facing the affordable housing shortage the bill described gained nothing from this bill's fate.

for.name: Rep. Julian C. Dixon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the original cosponsor list.

for.name: 30 of 267 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 30 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remaining fourteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill drew no recorded Republican support before dying in committee.

industries.industry: Low-income housing tax credit investors, syndicators, and affordable housing developers
industries.note: The bill makes the tax credit permanent, raises it to 9% for federally subsidized new construction, and exempts it from passive loss limits, locking in private investors and syndicators as the permanent channel through which federal affordable-housing support flows. More affordable housing would get built, but a meaningful share of the subsidy is captured by investors and intermediaries.

industries.industry: Rental property owners and real estate investors generally
industries.note: Faster 20-year depreciation and the passive loss exemption raise after-tax returns for owners of low-income buildings, and Section 6 extends passive loss relief to taxes, interest, and business expenses for actively participating owners. But Section 5 denies every deduction, including depreciation, for units not fit for occupancy.

Section 5 bars all tax deductions on rental units that are not suitable for occupancy under local health, safety, and building codes, targeting owners who collect rent from deteriorated units while claiming federal write-offs. This provision directly works against tenants living in substandard conditions.
